chief_complaint: bumped head in basketball, mild headache, no LOC
hpi_details: A 29-year-old male presents to the clinic with bumped head in basketball, mild headache, no loc. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
ideas: He thinks he took a hard elbow to the temple during his basketball game and gave his head a mild jolt.
concerns: He is worried that there could be slow internal bleeding in his head that might make him lose consciousness in his sleep tonight.
expectations: He hopes the doctor will check his eyes and reflexes, confirm he is safe to go home, and give him a sick note for work tomorrow.

clinical_knowledge.topic: Concussion (Mild Traumatic Brain Injury) evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Concussion (Mild Traumatic Brain Injury) is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Standard management emphasizes Plan for Concussion Head Injury: Apply Canadian CT Head Rule (not indicated), adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: bumped head in basketball, mild headache, no LOC

Key HPI features: A 29-year-old male presents to the clinic with bumped head in basketball, mild headache, no loc. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
Objective/Exam findings: Focused physical exam and vital signs check. Tailored diagnostics for Concussion Head Injury.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Concussion (Mild Traumatic Brain Injury).
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Intracranial hemorrhage without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Worsening symptoms.
management_principles: Plan for concussion: perform neurologic assessment and apply the Canadian CT Head Rule only after confirming eligibility and all high- and medium-risk features
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective:
Chief Complaint: bumped head in basketball, mild headache, no LOC

A 29-year-old male presents to the clinic with bumped head in basketball, mild headache, no loc. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
reference_soap.objective: Focused physical exam and vital signs check. Tailored diagnostics for Concussion Head Injury.
reference_soap.assessment: Condition highly suspicious for Concussion Head Injury.
reference_soap.plan: Perform neurologic assessment and apply the Canadian CT Head Rule only after confirming eligibility and all high- and medium-risk features; obtain CT if indicated. Provide written return precautions for worsening headache, repeated vomiting, seizure, confusion, focal weakness, or drowsiness. Recommend 24-48 hours of relative rest followed by a graded return to activity; no same-day return to sport.

must_ask.say: Have you had a concussion before?

history.answer: I bumped my head while playing basketball earlier today, and I have had a dull headache and felt really worn out since then.
Another player and I collided going for a rebound about two hours ago, and his head hit the left side of my forehead.
No, I did not pass out or lose consciousness at all; I was awake the whole time.
I remember everything before, during, and right after the collision clearly without any gaps.
The headache started right after the bump as a mild ache, but it has been gradually getting worse over the past couple of hours.
It has been aching continuously for the past two hours, and I do not usually get headaches like this.
It is mainly across the front of my head and around my left forehead where I was hit.
It feels like a dull, throbbing pressure, maybe around a 3 or 4 out of 10.
Moving around and bright lights make it throb more, while sitting quietly in a dim room helps a little.
I feel surprisingly exhausted and a little foggy, but I have not had any neck pain or ringing in my ears.
I felt slightly queasy right after it happened, but I have not thrown up at all.
Yes, bright lights and loud gym noises were bothering me, so I had to sit out.
No, I did not see any flashing lights, zigzag lines, or have any tingling before the headache started.
No blurred vision, double vision, or pain behind my eyes.
No, my arms and legs feel completely normal, no numbness, speech trouble, or shaking spells.
No eye watering, redness, or runny nose.
No fever, chills, neck stiffness, or skin rashes.
No, this is the first time I have ever had a head injury or concussion.
I have not taken any pain medications yet because I wanted to get checked out first.
No lack of sleep or unusual stress; the pain was triggered directly by the blow to my head.
I do not have high blood pressure, and I do not take any blood thinners or aspirin.
None of my teammates or family members have headaches, and we were playing in an open gymnasium.
No, I have never had cancer or any immune system problems.
I think I just took an elbow to the side of my head going for a rebound and gave myself a bit of a bump.
I'm worried that there could be hidden bleeding inside my skull that might get worse when I fall asleep tonight.
I'm hoping you can check my reflexes and pupils to make sure it's safe for me to sleep, and write me a doctor's note for work tomorrow.
I have always been healthy and have no chronic medical conditions.
I have never had surgery or been admitted to a hospital.
I do not take any prescription medications or over-the-counter supplements.
I have no known allergies to medications, foods, or anything else.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used tobacco products.
I only drink socially, maybe one or two beers on the weekend, but none today.
I work in an office as an accountant and live in an apartment with my roommate.
My parents are both healthy in their fifties, and there is no family history of migraines or brain diseases.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 122/78 mmHg, heart rate 72 beats per minute, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute, temperature 36.8°C, and oxygen saturation 99% on room air.
Alert and oriented young male sitting comfortably without acute distress, appearing mildly fatigued.
Mild localized tenderness over a small contusion on the left frontal scalp, with no laceration, depression, or signs of basilar skull fracture.
Glasgow Coma Scale score of 15, fully alert and oriented to person, place, and time, with intact immediate and delayed recall.
Neck is supple with full range of motion; Kernig and Brudzinski signs are negative.
Pupils are equal, round, and briskly reactive to light; extraocular movements are intact without nystagmus, and fundoscopy reveals sharp disc margins with no papilledema.
Cranial nerves II through XII are grossly intact with symmetric facial sensation and movement.
Muscle bulk and tone are normal, with 5/5 motor strength throughout all four limbs.
Sensation to light touch and pinprick is intact and symmetric across all extremities.
Deep tendon reflexes are 2+ and symmetric bilaterally; plantar responses are flexor.
Normal finger-to-nose testing, steady tandem gait, and negative Romberg test.
No tenderness elicited over the frontal or maxillary sinuses.
No cervical midline spinal tenderness, step-off, or paraspinal muscle spasms.
